title: Central banks on pause for now but policy divergence is coming
gist: Capital Economics argues central banks will all hold this week in response to the Iran oil shock, but that the common policy path markets price - just over 50bps of hikes in the US, UK and euro-zone by mid-2027 - is wrong. With US core PCE near 3.3%, loose fiscal policy and AI investment adding to demand, the Fed should hike three times by mid-2027 (starting September) while the BoE holds and may cut, and the ECB unwinds its hike, implying an autumn rates repricing and a stronger dollar.

themes.theme: Stagflationary oil shock: why the default answer is to do nothing

insights.claim: The Iran war is a classic stagflationary supply shock that pushes inflation up while weighing on growth in energy-importing economies, and there is no clean monetary policy response to it.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Don't expect rate decisions to 'solve' the oil shock; trade the pass-through and the reaction function instead of the headline.
insights.quote: Higher oil prices amount to a classic stagflationary supply shock: they push inflation up while weighing on growth, particularly in energy-importing economies. There is no obvious monetary policy response.
insights.locator: The Iran war has presented central banks

insights.claim: Central banks can only offset demand shocks with policy; against a supply shock like higher oil, tightening merely destroys demand elsewhere in the economy rather than adding supply.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Frames why hikes into an oil spike are about credibility signalling, not inflation control - a key tell for fading knee-jerk rate repricing.
insights.quote: Raising interest rates cannot produce more oil. It can only weaken demand elsewhere in the economy.
insights.locator: Energy prices not the inflation threat they were

insights.claim: The ECB set the template last week by acknowledging inflation risks and warning on second-round effects while leaving policy unchanged, and the Federal Reserve and Bank of England are expected to repeat it with no change in rates at this week's meetings.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Base case is three holds this week; the signal is in the guidance and in oil, not the rate decision.
insights.quote: The Federal Reserve and the Bank of England are likely to follow the same playbook at their meetings this week. We expect no change in interest rates from either.
insights.locator: The European Central Bank set the tone last week

insights.claim: Higher energy prices historically take six to twelve months to feed meaningfully into wage settlements and broader price-setting, so the absence of second-round effects so far is uninformative.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Gives a timing window: judge pass-through from spring 2027 data, not from the next two CPI prints.
insights.quote: Historically, it takes six to twelve months for higher energy prices to feed meaningfully into wage settlements and broader price-setting behaviour.

insights.claim: Advanced-economy labour markets are no longer as tight as after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine and survey measures of excess demand show economies running nowhere near as hot, which should limit how much this energy shock becomes persistent domestic inflation.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Argues against a 2022-style inflation spiral, supporting duration and fading inflation-breakeven spikes on oil headlines.
insights.quote: Labour markets across the advanced economies are no longer as tight as they were back then and survey measures of excess demand suggest that most advanced economies are running nowhere near as hot as they once were.

themes.theme: Reaction function beats the data: Brent $120 as the trigger level

insights.claim: Forecasting central banks now requires modelling their reaction function rather than just the economic outlook, because officials caught on the back foot in the 2022 inflation shock are biased toward not repeating that mistake.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Skew is asymmetric toward hawkish surprises even where the macro data argues for patience.
insights.quote: Having been caught on the back foot during the inflation shock of 2022, central bankers are understandably wary of making the same mistake again.

insights.claim: If the Iran war continues and Brent crude climbs toward roughly $120 per barrel over the summer, policymakers will face rising pressure to hike purely to demonstrate commitment to their inflation targets, even though a single 25bp move would barely change the inflation outlook.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Gives a tradeable oil threshold: use ~$120 Brent as the trigger for repricing hawkish central bank risk.
insights.quote: if the Iran war continues and Brent crude were to climb towards, say, $120 per barrel over the summer, policymakers would come under increasing pressure to demonstrate that they remain committed to their inflation targets

themes.theme: The divergence trade: markets are mispricing a common path

insights.claim: Markets are pricing broadly similar policy-rate paths across the major advanced economies, with just over 50bps of hikes priced in the US, UK and euro-zone by mid-2027, even as their economic backdrops diverge sharply.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: The setup for relative-value rates trades: pay US front-end versus receive UK and euro-zone.
insights.quote: currently just over 50bps of hikes in the US, UK and euro-zone by mid-2027
insights.locator: Another way in which the US is exceptional

insights.claim: Underlying domestic inflation pressures are much weaker in the UK and euro-zone, and UK unemployment is expected to start edging back up in the second half of this year despite signs of labour market stabilisation, so the Bank of England and ECB will deliver less tightening than investors expect.
insights.speaker: Capital Economics
insights.so_what: Receive UK and euro-zone rates; the priced tightening is hard to justify if oil falls back.
insights.quote: We continue to think the Bank of England and the ECB will ultimately deliver less tightening than investors currently expect.
